issues.legal_issue: A uniform per-acre drainage levy within each area division, with different rates between divisions reflecting their drainage needs and costs, does not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality.
material_facts: The levy funded drainage and flood-control schemes intended to protect lands across the delta area.
The drainage and flood problems, proposed works, and estimated costs varied between parts of the area.
The area was divided into four units using geographical features, drainage characteristics, and the improvements and expenditure required in each unit.
The levy imposed a uniform rate per acre within each unit, while rates differed between units in accordance with the estimated cost of their schemes.

The drainage schemes benefited irrigated lands through flood protection and improved drainage; differences in the degree of benefit to particular landowners arose from their land’s location and susceptibility to flooding.
issues.conclusion: The classification and levy were not discriminatory, and the provisions did not violate Article 14 of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: A taxing law is subject to Article 14, but the legislature has wide latitude to make reasonable classifications for taxation. The classification must rest on an intelligible differentia with a rational connection to the law’s object; a complainant must show hostile unequal treatment, not merely possible inequality. Where equality and uniformity exist within a group, fortuitous differences in the advantages individual members receive do not alone make the law discriminatory. The Court applied Khandige Sham Bhat v. Agricultural Income-tax Officer, East India Tobacco Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Twyford Tea Co. Ltd. v. State of Kerala, and Vivian Joseph Ferreira v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay. It distinguished Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala, State of Andhra Pradesh v. Nalla Raja Reddy, New Manek Chowk Spinning and Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Ahmedabad, and State of Kerala v. Haji K. Haji K. Kutty Naha; it also relied on the classification guidance in Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_tax_classification and drainage_levy_funds_area_wide_protection and divisions_track_drainage_needs_and_costs and uniform_per_acre_burden_within_each_division and different_rates_track_division_costs

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_tax_classifi: A person challenged a tax classification as unequal treatment.
predicates.drainage_levy_funds_area_wide_protection: The levy funded drainage or flood-control works intended to protect lands across an area.
predicates.divisions_track_drainage_needs_and_costs: The area was divided into units according to differences in drainage needs and the cost of required works.
predicates.uniform_per_acre_burden_within_each_divi: Every acre within each unit was charged at the same rate.
predicates.different_rates_track_division_costs: The rates differed between units in a manner reflecting the estimated cost of works in each unit.

issues.definition: When a tax-classification challenge concerns an area-wide protective scheme, and the divisions and rates reflect differing needs and costs while applying a uniform per-acre burden within each division, the classification is not discriminatory.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory right to appeal a levy is not illusory merely because the appellate authority cannot alter a rate fixed by law, when the appeal can contest the land area assessed or its ownership.
material_facts: A person aggrieved by the levy could appeal after receiving notice requiring payment.
An appellant could dispute the area on which the levy was imposed or who owned that area, including whether the assessed area exceeded the land owned or had been transferred.
The rate was fixed by the statute and the related notification, rather than left to the appellate authority to determine.
issues.conclusion: The statutory right of appeal was not illusory.
issues.legal_principle: The appeal provision allowed an aggrieved person to contest matters such as the area assessed and its ownership. The appellate authority’s inability to determine a different rate did not make the appeal illusory. The Court considered the notice and appeal mechanisms in sections 4 and 5 of the Act.

predicates.challenge_to_statutory_appeal_right: A person challenged whether a statutory appeal from a levy provided a real opportunity for review.
predicates.appeal_can_test_assessed_area_or_ownersh: The appeal allowed the person to dispute the area assessed or ownership of that area.
predicates.rate_is_fixed_outside_the_appeal: The rate was fixed by law or by an authority other than the appellate body.

issues.definition: If a challenged appeal can review the assessed area or its ownership, the appeal is not illusory merely because the rate is fixed outside that appeal.

issues.legal_issue: Delegating the setting of a tax rate within a statutory maximum is not excessive merely because the statute sets no minimum, when it provides sufficient guidance for fixing the rate.
material_facts: The statute set a maximum rate but did not set a minimum rate.
It authorized the government to specify the rate within that maximum.
The rate for a division was guided by the expenditure required for the drainage scheme in that division.
The government specified a rate at the statutory maximum.
issues.conclusion: There was no excessive delegation of legislative power, and the absence of a minimum rate did not invalidate the taxing law.
issues.legal_principle: The legislature may prescribe a maximum rate and authorize the designated authority to levy up to that limit. The absence of a statutory minimum does not by itself invalidate a taxing statute. Here, the Act provided guidance by tying the rate in each division to the expenditure for that division’s drainage scheme. The Court referred to section 3 and the statutory schedule, and to the discussion in Cooley’s Law of Taxation on legislative limits on taxation.

rule.if: challenge_to_delegated_tax_rate_setting and statute_sets_a_maximum_rate and statute_sets_no_minimum_rate and rate_is_guided_by_scheme_expenditure and administering_authority_stays_within_maximum

predicates.challenge_to_delegated_tax_rate_setting: A person challenged the legislature’s delegation of authority to set a tax rate.
predicates.statute_sets_a_maximum_rate: The law fixed an upper limit on the rate that could be imposed.
predicates.statute_sets_no_minimum_rate: The law did not fix a lower limit on the rate.
predicates.rate_is_guided_by_scheme_expenditure: The law guided the rate by reference to expenditure required for the relevant scheme.
predicates.administering_authority_stays_within_max: The authority setting the rate imposed no rate above the statutory upper limit.

issues.definition: When a challenged rate-setting delegation has a statutory ceiling and expenditure-based guidance, the absence of a minimum and the authority’s compliance with the ceiling do not make the delegation excessive.
